Photograph: Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters View image in fullscreen A woman prepares food at a field kitchen set up by the local authorities to provide residents with hot meals in the settlement of Massandra, Crimea, where Ukraine has succeeded in cutting off power and fuel supplies. Photograph: Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Strikes on three Russian oil refineries and sanctioned ship Power cut to Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant; meal queues in Crimea where Ukrainian strikes have cut fuel and power supplies. What we know on day 1,621 Warren Murray and agencies Sat 1 Aug 2026 21.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 21.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian drones struck three oil refineries in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan , Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. The refineries “process millions of tonnes of oil each year” and are located nearly 1,600km (994 miles) from Ukraine , Ukraine’s president said. The Russian online news outlet Astra reported Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set on fire an oil refinery in Ufa, the capital of Bashkortostan. A sanctioned Russian container ship, the Yanina, sank in the Black Sea after being hit by Ukrainian drones, Zelenskyy said, listing the ship as among “facilities that sustain the war effort”. Russia’s state nuclear energy company, Rosatom, whose shipping subsidiary FESCO operates the vessel, claimed the ship was carrying “civilian goods” such as frozen food and construction materials. Laura Loomer, Lindsey Graham and the deepening Iran crisis: what’s behind Trump’s reset with Zelenskyy? Read more The ⁠International Atomic Energy ⁠Agency (IAEA) ⁠said on ​Saturday that Ukraine’s ⁠ Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant ⁠lost ​off-site ‌power ‌for nearly two hours – the 23rd ‌time it has happened since the full-scale Russian invasion. The plant is illegally occupied by Russia and not operating, but needs power supplied from outside to power cooling systems that maintain the safety of its nuclear materials. Ukraine’s campaign to cut off illegally occupied Crimea from Russia has led to people having to queue in the streets for hot meals due to power cuts , Reuters reports. It caught up with residents waiting in the town of Massandra for food being cooked in huge pots. Standing beside boiling vats of buckwheat, later to be added to plates of reheated tinned beef, Massandra town administration head Oksana Madyud said her workers were serving roughly 200 people per day, “as under the current circumstances not everyone has the means to cook hot food on electric ​hobs”. Ukraine says it is “bringing the war back home to ‌Russia” by striking deep inside the country, as well as hitting territory the invader controls and has sought to populate with Russian immigrants . View image in fullscreen People line up for meals at a field kitchen in Massandra, Crimea. Photograph: Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters One local woman, Marina, said a bad leg made the climb down from her 10th-floor apartment difficult, but the lack of electricity had sent her hunting for a gas cooker and ⁠some cylinders. Another older resident, ​Alexandra, said she had been lured down by the ​smell of the ‌lunch after ​ going without ​electricity for 10 days . “They turned it back on today, at 4 o’clock” in the afternoon, but she wasn’t sure the lights would still be on when she returned home, she added. Lithuania’s foreign minister said on Saturday that its embassy in Kyiv was damaged when Russian missiles struck nearby. The Lithuanian foreign ministry said there were no injuries but embassy windows broke, solar collectors were damaged and the yard was scattered with debris. The minister, Kestutis Budrys, said: “Today we will summon the Russian ​embassy representative to protest. We understand this won’t stop this madness and ⁠aggression against Ukraine. What might stop it ​is ​continued support to Ukraine, ​raising its resilience and ​piling ‌pressure on ​Russia through ​sanctions so it finally sits at the negotiation table.” Recovery efforts continued in Kyiv after a Russian missile and drone barrage killed at least nine people and wounded 33 civilians over Friday night and into Saturday. A five-story residential building in the city’s Solomianskyi district was damaged and a fire broke out. Rescue workers evacuated 35 people from the upper floors of the building and two people died, with eight reported injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s state emergency service. View image in fullscreen A Russian missile strike partially destroyed an apartment block in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district. Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock In the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv, seven people were killed and another 14 injured after the attack caused fires and damage to houses, vehicles, an administrative and non-residential building, the emergency services said. Elsewhere, emergency workers extinguished a fire in a non-residential building in the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district. There was no additional information about earlier reports by the district mayor that people were trapped in another residential building. A Russian airstrike killed one person and wounded five more in the city of Kherson in southern Ukraine, local officials said on Saturday. Zelenskyy posted a further plea for Patriot missiles. “Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties.” Due to the air defence shortages, Ukraine was only able to shoot down one out of the 27 ballistic missiles in Friday night’s barrage, Zelenskyy said. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-short.text: Brussels is seeking to bring down housing costs in Europe’s most popular cities by giving local governments the tools to rein in Airbnb and other short-term rental operators. As part of the European Commission’s Affordable Housing Act , due to be approved on Wednesday, EU-wide rules will determine whether an area is under housing stress , and national, regional and local authorities will be given legal backing to use targeted measures to ease home shortages. “Short-term rentals are not the cause of Europe’s housing crisis,” Energy and Housing Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told POLITICO. “But it’s very clear that in some parts of Europe, especially in some of our biggest cities, they are aggravating the problem.” Advertisement Advertisement While registered short-term rentals officially account for around only 1.2 percent of the bloc’s overall housing stock , they can make up as much as 20 percent of homes in tourist hotspots like Porto and major European cities. According to consulting firm AirDNA, there were roughly 60,000 active short-term rental listings in Paris last year, while short-term rental listings accounted for nearly 40 percent of available rental stock in central Porto, and as much as 56 percent of the long-term rental stock in some Madrid neighborhoods. “Where thousands of homes are taken out of the residential market in an already stressed city, we cannot pretend this has no effect on affordability and availability of homes,” Jørgensen said. “People should be able to afford to live and stay in the communities they call home.” People before profit Many cities are already attempting to tackle short-term rentals. Barcelona plans to phase out its roughly 10,000 licensed tourist apartments by 2028, while Amsterdam, Florence and Paris have introduced licensing systems , rental caps or limits on new short-term lets . But those efforts have often triggered long legal battles. Homeowners and tourism operators sued Florence over its restrictions, and Airbnb challenged a €64 million fine Spain imposed after determining the platform included illegal listings. While both efforts proved unsuccessful, they left local governments tied up in court. Advertisement Advertisement But those efforts have often triggered legal action. Homeowners and tourism operators sued Florence over its restrictions, and Airbnb challenged a €64 million fine imposed by Spain after authorities determined the platform was carrying illegal listings. Although courts ruled in favor of the city governments, the lawsuits nevertheless tied up local authorities in costly, protracted court battles. Jørgensen said the new legislation would “give the possibility to local authorities which want to take action, to do so in a way that is effective and that does not expose them to litigation risks.” The commissioner rejected industry allegations that restrictions could hurt tourism-dependent economies and homeowners who depend on rental income, insisting that “housing is a right, not just a commodity” and “people need to come before profit.” He also dismissed industry claims that the Commission is overreaching by legislating on housing, an area where the EU has limited direct competence. Jørgensen pointed out that, under the new plans, national, regional and local authorities will determine which areas are under housing stress and decide whether and how to intervene. “The goal is not to impose restrictions from Brussels,” he said. “But housing affordability is one of Europe’s most pressing challenges and European institutions cannot be blind to the very concrete daily problems our citizens are facing.” “If we fail to address this crisis, we risk losing our people’s trust in democratic institutions,” he added. “And that would lead to the rise of extremist political forces .” The legislation comes almost one year after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the EU’s housing shortage as a “social crisis” and pledged to take action. Jørgensen said the new act represented a “key step to support cities, regions and countries that want to bring immediate solutions to the areas and the people most affected,” but stressed that it was not a panacea. “The housing crisis is a complex issue,” he said, adding that the bloc still needed to “act on investment, simplification of rules, supply and pressures on the existing housing stock.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: People take part in a demonstration in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, where hundreds of people have set up camp to protest against Abascal’s eviction. Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPA View image in fullscreen People take part in a demonstration in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, where hundreds of people have set up camp to protest against Abascal’s eviction. Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPA Spain Spain announces plan to ease housing crisis amid outcry over eviction of 87-year-old Measures, which need to be approved in Congress, include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.27 EDT First published on Tue 29 Sep 2026 09.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week. Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible. Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028. A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements. View image in fullscreen Maricarmen Abascal attends an event organised by housing activists the day before her scheduled eviction from her home in Madrid. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Maricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after she was evicted from her Madrid home on Wednesday. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters Hundreds of people remained camped out in ⁠one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the ⁠automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes. It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree. Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.” She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.” ‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis Read more The Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees. “It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.” View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police near the Puerta del Sol encampment in Madrid. Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to ‌it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.” View image in fullscreen Housing rights protesters remain camped at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Photograph: Mario Mor ³N/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.” Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction. View image in fullscreen A protester in the encampment at Puerta del Sol. The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Underlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband. Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/orb.text: The Budapest Times Orbán drops the mask: ‘national resistance’ and a seven-point plan to retake power The time for national resistance has come, patience is over, goodwill is over, every unilateral gesture is over — the gauntlet must be picked up and the fight must be joined, the president of Fidesz declared in a speech at the Kötcse gathering of the party's intellectual circle, based on an audio recording published on the Vadhajtások YouTube channel. Speaking about his party's defeat at the meeting, Viktor Orbán said that in a difficult political situation they had failed to find the right answer to a very difficult puzzle, and remarked of the prime minister that he should not be taken seriously because he talks incoherently. At the event held on 12 September, Viktor Orbán said: the leading force of national resistance today is Fidesz, and I believe it will remain so. He stressed that only they possess the necessary knowledge, organisation, resources, leadership, and parliamentary presence. He stated that Fidesz’s role is to support everyone willing to raise their voice against tyranny and willing to fight, “including the left.” He added that it is forbidden to support anyone who moves against another right-wing group, because such activity is “harmful.” Common causes, a common language, mutual loyalty, a unified national camp, confronting the government with reality, “mapping the true nature of the new communist regime” — the president of Fidesz listed the tasks of the autumn in a speech of approximately one hour. Viktor Orbán spoke about how “if a miracle does not happen, the economy will hit a wall,” and that the government’s disintegration would come faster than expected, meaning they must be prepared for that situation. Naming the task as getting into government, he outlined the steps necessary to achieve this in seven points. As he said, they have largely finished the task of “clearing the rubble” and taking stock. Now comes the consolidation of their organisation and its role among right-wing voters, after which they must secure a majority in society. “We are very far from that,” he said, indicating that there is a chance of achieving it only when there are more discontented people than satisfied ones. He named the final step as converting all of this into a majority of votes. Any breach of this order will have serious consequences, Viktor Orbán declared, emphasising that the dynamics of the process depend on their own work and the pace of “the government’s collapse.” “In difficult times we have an incompetent government,” in difficult times there are bad government decisions, in difficult times there are weak government figures, as a result of which the economy has been paralysed — in the best case there is a wait-and-see attitude across the entire economy, or a complete standstill. This will have serious consequences, assessed the president of Fidesz. He said that in such a situation, the head of the Hungarian economy is an “energy trader” who has never dealt with macroeconomics, and that while the finance minister is “very easy to have a conversation with,” he is “a weak leader who gets pushed around.” According to Viktor Orbán’s prognosis, the deterioration of the situation will be signalled first by municipal bankruptcies, then by insolvencies in the agricultural sector and among small and medium-sized enterprises, followed by mounting problems for pensioners — with the end result being a “completely paralysed economy, one that is shaken in its macroeconomic indicators as well.” In the government’s words, its complete incompetence and incapacity is “by its very nature only temporarily concealable.” Viktor Orbán spoke about how the right’s mission is to achieve a sovereign state, while Tisza’s is to “turn Hungary into a colony once again.” He projected that after taking over politics, they would hand over the “economy that had been re-Magyarised with great difficulty” to foreigners. That is the essence of the deal, the essence of colonial existence, he said. “Reality is the ally of the right,” he declared, expressing his view that “the tradition” of a prime minister being, by definition, a serious person “has ceased to exist.” The prime minister should not be taken seriously, because he speaks incoherently, he said, adding that it is not Péter Magyar’s words that matter, but what is actually happening. He mentioned that the right had always agreed on three things: the necessity of sovereignty, the conviction that “there is no life without freedom,” and that the legacy they had received is a value that must be carried forward. He stressed that the right had always been a mosaic community, and had sought a leader who could fit these elements together in such a way as to produce victory. Speaking about the period since the election, he said it had been a difficult five months, representing at once a political, character, and — for many — an existential test, but that “the loss of manpower is below all expectations, between 5 and 10 percent,” as the composition of participants shows. Addressing the reasons for the defeat, he said that in a difficult political situation they had failed to find the right answer to a very difficult puzzle — not at the level of strategy, nor tactics, nor communication, nor technology. He said that the majority of voters did not accept the strategic message that we are living in an age of dangers and that security takes precedence over everything else, while at the tactical level the opponent “convinced people that choice is good and that choice represents an opportunity.” In terms of communication, he highlighted that instead of the shorter campaign format customary in previous elections, the prime minister was sent on a lengthy country-touring campaign, adding that the effectiveness of the digital civic circles fell short of the rival’s online presence. He stressed that a distinction must be drawn between the election result and the assessment of 16 years of governance. “There were bad things even when we won, and now that we have lost, not everything was bad either,” Viktor Orbán declared. Regarding the National Asset Protection and Asset Recovery Office, which he referred to as the ÁVH, Viktor Orbán stated that it must be made clear that politicians cannot be held responsible for the establishment of the new institution, but that anyone who “went there and made decisions is subject to criminal and financial liability” and cannot escape accountability. https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/dylan-sp.text: Culture Dylan Sprouse and Barbara Palvin welcome their 1st baby together 1:14 Barbara Palvin Sprouse returns to the Victoria’s Secret runway after health battle Aurore Marechal/Getty Images By Angeline Jane Bernabe September 28, 2026, 7:22 PM By Angeline Jane Bernabe September 28, 2026, 7:22 PM Dylan Sprouse and Barbara Palvin have entered their parent era. The couple announced in an Instagram post on Monday that they welcomed their first baby together on Labor Day. "We took Labor Day literally this year 👼🏻," Palvin wrote in the caption of a joint post with Sprouse. Related Dylan Sprouse, Barbara Palvin share pregnancy announcement In the photo, the couple wears Dodgers jerseys and face a TV screen as a Dodger game plays. In Sprouse's arms is their baby, who is also wearing a Dodgers shirt. Barbara Sprouse and Dylan Sprouse attend the Grand Dîner du Louvre at Musee du Louvre on March 03, 2026 in Paris, France. Aurore Marechal/Getty Images ABC News has reached out to a representative for Palvin and Sprouse for comment. A rep for Palvin confirmed ot ABC News in May that she and Sprouse were expecting. Today's 10 deals starting at 40% off: Madewell, Bath & Body Works, and more 8 hours ago Michael Douglas reflects on marriage 'time out' with Catherine Zeta-Jones Oct 6 Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 2 days ago The duo had shared an Instagram post about the news with a sonogram image showing a tiny hand making a rock 'n' roll hand gesture. Sprouse and Palvin were married on July 15, 2023, in Palvin's home country of Hungary. In August, Sprouse appeared on Amanda Hirsch's Not Skinny but Not Fat podcast and recalled how he met Palvin at a party where she had cut him in line for the red carpet. He said the moment felt like a rom-com. "I was like, 'I don't care how pretty you are, you're not cutting me,'" Sprouse said. "And she turns around, and I'm wearing this red and white striped shirt, and she goes, 'What, are you a hot dog vendor?'" Last year, Palvin shared in an Instagram post that she'd had surgery for endometriosis. Related Dylan Sprouse, Barbara Palvin open up about engagement, upcoming wedding "For some years now I've been dealing with the difficulties that can come with my periods. Fatigue, severe pain, heavy and irregular flow, sleepless nights on the bathroom floor. I thought this was just how it works for me," she wrote at the time. She continued, "[The surgery] helped me a lot, and I'm grateful I did it. Early diagnosis and treatment are very important to prevent long-term complications, and now I'm more mindful about my body to act fast if needed." Palvin ended the August post by saying she was "excited about this new chapter of my life and now ready to get back to work." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6re.text: By Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer BBC Verify Published 5 hours ago An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas. Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran . The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed. UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black. The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts". Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage. Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October. But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR. Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish. They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce. Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation. But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish. The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory. Tanker hit 14 days ago BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2. Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished. Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship. Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea. The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media. All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October. Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October . Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane. Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries. Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August , which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities. Its adoption showcases Moscow’s ability to secure diplomatic support against economic pressure while retaining a Security Council veto over action concerning its own conduct. by Lesia Dubenko | Oct. 10, 2026, 5:03 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied This photograph shows a general view during the 63rd session of United Nations (UN) Human Rights Council, in Geneva, on September 7, 2026. (Photo by Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Russia and Uganda have helped secure a UN Human Rights Council resolution declaring unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, giving Moscow another diplomatic argument against sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine. Adopted by 27 votes to 16, with four abstentions , the resolution extends for three years the mandate of the special rapporteur examining the negative human rights effects of such measures. Uganda sponsored the draft on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, alongside Russia. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Neither sponsor is currently a Human Rights Council member, so neither participated in the vote. Their role nevertheless illustrates how Moscow can influence UN proceedings beyond the Security Council, where it holds a permanent seat and veto. Advertisement What the resolution says about sanctions The resolution’s preamble declares unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, international humanitarian law, and the UN Charter. Its operative provisions renew the rapporteur’s mandate and request continued institutional support. The text does not itself overturn sanctions against Russia or determine the legality of individual restrictions. It sustains a UN mechanism focused on their adverse human rights effects, whose work Moscow can invoke when challenging economic pressure. That broad framing leaves important distinctions between sanctions unresolved. The EU’s restrictions on Russia target military-industrial capacity alongside revenue and other resources supporting the war. They also include exemptions and safeguards for humanitarian needs and essential civilian supplies. Other Topics of Interest ‘I Love the Smell of Russian Gas’: Controversial Polish Politician Backs Nord Stream Grzegorz Braun urged Poland to help revive Nord Stream during an appearance with Germany’s far-right AfD, drawing accusations of “shame and treason.” While those provisions do not eliminate the need to investigate civilian harm, assessing it requires examining the purpose, scope, and implementation of particular restrictions. For Moscow, a general condemnation offers a broader argument against measures adopted outside the Security Council, where Russia can block their authorization. Advertisement Russia’s veto limits collective action As a permanent Security Council member, Russia can veto substantive resolutions, including those authorizing sanctions against it. Moscow demonstrated its willingness to obstruct action concerning its own conduct on Feb. 25, 2022, vetoing a draft resolution that condemned its invasion and demanded the withdrawal of Russian forces . The Human Rights Council resolution does not explicitly declare that only Security Council sanctions are legitimate. However, treating council authorization as a prerequisite would make sanctions against Russia dependent on overcoming Russia’s own veto. Moscow thus benefits from two complementary positions: it can prevent Security Council action while supporting arguments elsewhere in the UN against pressure imposed outside that body. This selective approach also appears in Russia’s broader use of international law . Moscow invokes legal protections when discussing Russian speakers abroad, yet disregarded the International Court of Justice’s March 2022 order to suspend the military operations it began in Ukraine on Feb. 24. Moscow can also block the next UN chief Russia’s institutional leverage extends to the selection of the secretary-general. As Kyiv Post’s examination of the succession process explains , a successful candidate needs a Security Council recommendation supported by at least nine members and vetoed by none of the five permanent members. Advertisement That gives Moscow the power to block a candidate to succeed António Guterres. It does not require Russia to vote in favor, since a permanent member’s abstention does not prevent a recommendation, but any candidate must avoid a Russian veto. Changing the underlying rules presents another obstacle. Under Article 108 of the UN Charter, amendments require adoption by two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent Security Council members. Russia can therefore obstruct Charter amendments that would remove its privileged position. A change in UN leadership alone would leave that constraint intact. Some backers had also supported Ukraine The sanctions resolution’s supporters have markedly different voting records on Ukraine. Of the 27 governments backing the text, 16 also supported the General Assembly’s February 2023 resolution calling for a just peace and Russia’s withdrawal . They included Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia, Egypt, Kenya, and the UAE. On the Ukraine-sponsored resolution adopted in February 2025 , however, only five of the same countries voted in favor: Egypt, Gambia, Indonesia, Mauritius, and Thailand. Eighteen abstained, Burundi and Sudan voted against, and Benin, Bolivia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not vote. Advertisement Brazil, Colombia, Kenya, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, and Zambia were among those that moved from supporting the 2023 text to abstaining in 2025. The latter resolution reaffirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity, recalled the demand for Russian withdrawal and called for accountability for crimes committed during the war. These votes concern different texts but they do show that condemnation of Russian aggression does not necessarily translate into support for economic pressure on Moscow. Scrutiny of Russia continues Other decisions made by the council show the limits of Moscow’s influence. During the same session, members voted 21-5, with 21 abstentions, to renew the special rapporteur’s mandate on human rights inside Russia . Independent scrutiny of Russian abuses therefore continues alongside the sanctions mechanism Moscow supported.
